entries.term: how big a, how good a, how much of a
entries.ipa: /ˌhaʊ ˈbɪɡ ə/, /ˌhaʊ ˈɡʊd ə/, /ˌhaʊ ˈmʌtʃ əv ə/
entries.meaning: Asks — or exclaims — how far along a scale a single countable thing sits: what size, what quality, or what degree of a thing it really is.
examples: How big a house do you actually need for three people?
How good a lawyer do you have to be to argue that in front of a jury?
How much of a problem is the noise going to be at night?
I hadn't realized how serious a mistake the second signature was.
How much of a difference does the premium gas really make?
How long a drive is it from the airport to the hotel?
She asked how big a deposit the landlord was going to want.
entries.pronunciation note: the article is always the weak /ə/ here and never surfaces as /eɪ/; of reduces to /əv/ and in fast speech to a single syllabic [ə], so how much of a problem runs to [haʊ ˈmʌtʃ əvə ˈprɑbləm]. How itself has no weak form
entries.русский: насколько большой / хороший / серьёзный — вопрос о степени; прилагательное встаёт перед a/an
entries.position: predeterminer — the degree phrase stands in front of a/an, which then does its ordinary job on the noun; how much of a is the of-partitive member of the same slot
entries.register: neutral in both speech and writing; how much of a is the more colloquial of the two frames
entries.type: interrogative (degree), and exclamative in the uninverted version
entries.goes with: singular countable nouns only, because the whole construction is built around a/an — how big a house, how good a teacher, how much of a problem. Never a plural (✗ how big a houses, ✗ how big houses) and never an uncountable (✗ how heavy a traffic); with those you drop back to the ordinary quantifiers, which take no article at all — how many houses, how much traffic. How much of a additionally wants a noun that can be graded: ✓ how much of a risk, ✓ how much of a difference, ✗ how much of a chair.
entries.with of: How big a and how good a take no of in edited writing: ✗ how big of a house. That said, how big of a is thoroughly established in spoken American English — Midland, Western, and increasingly general — and it is a real spoken pattern rather than a slip of logic; editors still delete it. How much of a is the one member of the trio where of is obligatory and standard: ✗ how much a problem is it?
entries.pattern: How [adjective] a/an [singular countable noun] [auxiliary] [subject] [verb]? · How much of a [singular countable noun] [verb]? · How [adjective] a/an [noun] [subject] [verb]! (exclamative, no inversion) · [clause] how [adjective] a/an [noun] [subject] [verb] (embedded, statement order) · spoken only: how [adjective] of a [noun]
entries.variants: how big of a, how good of a (spoken American, nonstandard in edited writing), that big a (informal), so/too/as + adjective + a (the statement partners)
entries.contrast: this is the one construction in English where the adjective jumps in front of the article: ordinary a big house inverts to how big a house, never ✗ a how big house. The statement partners are so, too, as — too big a risk, as good a time as any — and how is simply the question-and-exclamation member of that family. Against how (exclamative), the difference is whether a noun is present: How big the house is! has only an adjective and leaves the article behind, while How big a house it is! brings the noun along in front of it. Against what a, what an, where the wh- word takes the article directly and the adjective stays put: ✓ What a big house!, ✗ What big a house! And how big a against how much of a is a difference of scale type — how big a problem measures the problem, how much of a problem asks whether it counts as one at all.
entries.see also: so, too, as, how (exclamative), what a, what an, how much, a

entries.meaning: Asks — or, far more often, exclaims — about a small number, treating the smallness as the point.
examples: How few people actually read the terms is the frightening part.
How few votes does it take to block the motion?
You would be amazed how few restaurants downtown open on Mondays.
How few of these applicants have any lab experience?
It is shocking how few students can name their own senator.
How few hours can I sleep and still function at work?
entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on few, because the point of the phrase is the smallness
entries.русский: как мало (штук) — о малом числе счётных; чаще восклицание, чем настоящий вопрос
entries.position: central — the two words together fill one central-determiner slot
entries.register: neutral; more often rhetorical than a genuine request for a number
entries.goes with: plural countable nouns only — how few voters, how few options. Never an uncountable (✗ how few money → how little money) and never a singular countable (✗ how few voter).
entries.with of: Required before another determiner or a pronoun — how few of the applicants, how few of them. In that construction how few is a pronoun, not a determiner, and the noun inside the of-phrase keeps its own determiner. Never before a bare plural: ✗ how few of applicants.
entries.pattern: how few [plural countable] · how few of [the/these/my + plural noun] · how few of [them/us] · How few [plural countable] [verb]! (exclamative) · [clause] how few [plural countable] [subject] [verb] (embedded, statement order)
entries.contrast: how few is to plural countables what how little is to uncountables, and it is the loaded twin of how many. How many students showed up? is neutral and simply asks for a number; How few students showed up! presupposes that the number was small and usually registers dismay. The negative loading comes from bare few, which means 'not many' — and because the loading is the whole point, there is no ✗ how a few.
entries.see also: how little, how many, few, fewer

entries.meaning: Asks or exclaims about a small amount, with the smallness taken for granted.
examples: How little sleep can you get by on?
It is amazing how little money they spent on the whole trip.
How little notice do we actually have to give?
I had not realized how little time was left.
How little of the budget is left for marketing?
How little effort would it take just to answer the email?
entries.pronunciation note: the t is a flap in General American, so it comes out as how-LID-ul
entries.русский: как мало (о неисчисляемом) — о малом объёме; малость подразумевается заранее
entries.position: central — the two words fill one slot
entries.goes with: uncountable nouns only — how little time, how little sleep, how little evidence. Never a plural countable (✗ how little friends → how few friends). It also runs as a degree adverb with no noun at all (how little it matters), and that use is not a determiner.
entries.with of: Required before another determiner or a pronoun — how little of the budget, how little of it. How little is a pronoun there. Bare how little + bare uncountable takes no of.
entries.pattern: how little [uncountable] · how little of [the/this/my + uncountable] · How little [uncountable] [subject] [verb]! · how little [verb] (degree adverb, no noun)
entries.contrast: the uncountable partner of how few, and the loaded twin of how much. The noun test separates the determiner from the adverb: how little sleep do you need has a noun after it and is a determiner; how little he cares has none and is an adverb of degree. As with how few, the bare negative-loading form is the only one available: ✗ how a little.
entries.see also: how few, how much, little, less

entries.meaning: Asks for the number of a countable set.
examples: How many people are coming to dinner?
I don't know how many times I've explained this.
How many of these boxes can I recycle?
How many hours a week do you actually work?
She asked how many copies we needed.
How many pieces of ID does the DMV want?
entries.pronunciation note: how carries the accent when a noun follows, and the sentence nucleus lands on the noun: HOW many PEOPLE came?
entries.русский: сколько (штук) — вопрос о числе исчисляемых предметов
entries.position: central — the two words fill one slot
entries.goes with: plural countable nouns only — how many people, how many times. Never an uncountable (✗ how many money → how much money), never a singular countable (✗ how many person). A measure word makes an uncountable countable and brings how many back: how many gallons of gas, how many pieces of advice.
entries.with of: Required before another determiner or a pronoun — how many of the seats, how many of them. Never ✗ how many them and never ✗ how many of seats. In the of-construction how many is a pronoun.
entries.pattern: How many [plural noun] [auxiliary] [subject] [verb]? · How many [plural noun] [verb]? (subject question) · How many of [the/these/my + plural noun]? · [clause] how many [plural noun] [subject] [verb] (embedded, statement order) · How many? (pronoun, noun understood)
entries.contrast: how many is to plural countables what how much is to uncountables — the single most common countability error learners make. Against how few, how many is neutral and expects a number of any size. Note the answer types as well: how many is answered with a number, how much with an amount or a price. In a subject question the verb agrees with the plural noun, not with how many: ✓ How many people are coming?, ✗ How many people is coming?
entries.see also: how much, how few, how many of, how much of, many

entries.term: how many fewer, how much less
entries.meaning: Asks for the size of a decrease — how much smaller the number or the amount will be.
examples: How many fewer flights will the airline run this winter?
How much less sugar does the new recipe use?
I want to know how many fewer people showed up than last year.
How much less of the budget goes to overhead now?
How many fewer hours would you have to work?
How much less rent are you paying in the new place?
entries.pronunciation note: fewer is two syllables, /ˈfju.ɚ/, not fyoor
entries.русский: на сколько меньше — вопрос о величине убыли: fewer со счётными, less с неисчисляемыми
entries.position: how many / how much fills the central slot; fewer and less are postdeterminers inside the phrase
entries.register: neutral; common in analytical, business, and journalistic speech
entries.goes with: how many fewer + plural countable (how many fewer flights); how much less + uncountable (how much less sugar). The split is the ordinary fewer/less split, so ✗ how much less flights and ✗ how many fewer sugar. How much less also runs as a degree adverb with no noun (how much less does it cost?), which is not the determiner use.
entries.with of: Required before another determiner or a pronoun — how much less of the budget, how many fewer of them. Pronoun there, not determiner.
entries.pattern: How many fewer [plural noun] [auxiliary] [subject] [verb]? · How much less [uncountable] …? · How much less [adjective/adverb]? (degree) · … than [comparison]
entries.variants: how many less (widespread in speech, nonstandard in edited writing)
entries.contrast: the downward mirror of how many more and how much more. Fewer counts, less measures. In edited American English less with a plural countable (how many less calories, less calories) is a usage error — though it is extremely common in speech and is fully standard in the fixed expressions less than five miles and one less thing, where the plural is measured rather than counted.
entries.see also: how many more, how much more, fewer, less

entries.meaning: Asks for the number still to come, or the number in addition to a quantity already counted.
examples: How many more chairs do we need for the reception?
How many more times do I have to say it?
She wanted to know how many more applications were still unread.
How many more days until the deadline?
How many more of these do you have in the back?
How many more people can the elevator hold?
entries.pronunciation note: in an impatient question the accent jumps to more: how many MORE times?
entries.русский: сколько ещё (штук) — вопрос о числе сверх уже имеющегося; часто с досадой
entries.position: how many fills the central slot; more is a postdeterminer between it and the noun
entries.goes with: plural countable nouns only — how many more chairs, how many more times. Never an uncountable (✗ how many more water → how much more water).
entries.with of: Partitive how many more of the / of them is possible and is required before a pronoun; how many more is a pronoun there. Never before a bare plural: ✗ how many more of chairs.
entries.pattern: How many more [plural noun] [auxiliary] [subject] [verb]? · How many more [plural noun] are there? · How many more of [them/these]? · [clause] how many more [plural noun] [subject] [verb] (embedded) · How many more? (pronoun)
entries.contrast: pairs with how much more exactly as many pairs with much. Keep the determiner apart from the pronoun: a noun follows the determiner (how many more chairs), nothing follows the pronoun (how many more do we need?). Word order inside the phrase is fixed: ✓ how many more chairs, ✗ how more many chairs.
entries.see also: how much more, how many, how many fewer, how much less, more

entries.term: how many of, how much of
entries.meaning: Asks what part or what proportion of an already identified set or mass is involved.
examples: How many of the emails did you actually read?
How much of the budget is already committed?
How many of them showed up on time?
How much of this is he paying for himself?
I wonder how many of those reviews are real.
How much of the movie did you sleep through?
entries.pronunciation note: of is nearly always the weak /əv/, and in fast speech reduces to /ə/ — how many of them [ˌhaʊ ˈmɛni ə ðəm]
entries.русский: сколько из, какая часть из — партитив; это уже местоимение, а не определитель
entries.position: not a determiner slot at all: how many / how much heads its own noun phrase and the of-phrase completes it, so the following noun keeps its own determiner
entries.type: interrogative (partitive — a pronoun construction, not a determiner)
entries.goes with: how many of + a definite plural (of the emails, of these people, of them); how much of + a definite uncountable or a whole singular thing (of the money, of this pie, of it). The complement of of must already be determined: ✓ how many of the emails, ✗ how many of emails.
entries.with of: Of is the construction itself and is obligatory. Drop it and you are back to the determiner: how many emails, not ✗ how many the emails.
entries.pattern: How many of [the/these/my + plural noun] [auxiliary] [subject] [verb]? · How much of [the/this/my + uncountable] …? · How many of [them/us/you]? · How much of [it/that]? · embedded: [clause] how many of [noun phrase] [subject] [verb]
entries.contrast: this is the of test that runs through the whole file, in its clearest form. How many emails did you read is a determiner — the noun follows directly. How many of the emails did you read is a pronoun — an of-phrase follows and the noun inside it keeps its own determiner. The same split separates which from which of, and what from what of. Verb agreement follows the noun in the of-phrase: How many of the files were deleted?
entries.see also: how many, how much, which of, what of

entries.meaning: Asks for the amount, quantity, or price of something that is not counted in units.
examples: How much money do you have on you?
How much time do we have before the train?
She asked how much experience I had with Python.
How much salt does the recipe call for?
How much rent are you paying now?
How much of the report did you finish?
How much is that jacket in the window?
entries.pronunciation note: how takes the accent when a noun follows; standing alone as a price question the phrase is usually how MUCH?
entries.русский: сколько (о неисчисляемом), почём — вопрос об объёме, количестве или цене
entries.position: central — the two words fill one slot
entries.goes with: uncountable nouns only — how much money, how much time, how much sugar. Never a plural countable (✗ how much people → how many people) and never a singular countable (✗ how much chair). With no noun at all it is a pronoun or an adverb asking about price or degree (How much is it?, How much do you care?), not a determiner.
entries.with of: Required before another determiner or a pronoun — how much of the money, how much of it. Bare how much + bare uncountable takes no of: ✗ how much of money.
entries.pattern: How much [uncountable] [auxiliary] [subject] [verb]? · How much [uncountable] [verb]? (subject question) · How much of [the/this/my + uncountable]? · [clause] how much [uncountable] [subject] [verb] (embedded) · How much? (pronoun)
entries.contrast: how much is to uncountables what how many is to plural countables. Note also that how much is the price question in English — How much is that jacket? — where many other languages use their word for what; ✗ What costs the jacket? is a direct-translation error that never sounds native. In a subject question the verb is singular, matching the uncountable noun: ✓ How much money is left?, ✗ How much money are left?
entries.see also: how many, how little, how many of, how much of, much

entries.meaning: Asks for the additional amount — what remains to be added, endured, or paid.
examples: How much more time do you need?
How much more evidence does the jury want?
How much more money is this going to cost me?
I don't know how much more patience I have for this.
How much more work is left on the kitchen?
How much more of this do I have to sit through?
entries.русский: сколько ещё (о неисчисляемом) — вопрос о добавке; часто риторически, с раздражением
entries.position: how much fills the central slot; more is a postdeterminer between it and the noun
entries.goes with: uncountable nouns only — how much more time, how much more evidence. Never a plural countable (✗ how much more people → how many more people). It is also common with no noun at all, as a degree adverb (how much more expensive is it?) or an endurance question (how much more can I take?) — neither of those is the determiner use.
entries.with of: Partitive how much more of the / of this / of it is possible and is required before a pronoun, where how much more is a pronoun.
entries.pattern: How much more [uncountable] [auxiliary] [subject] [verb]? · How much more of [this/it]? · How much more [adjective]? (degree — how much more expensive) · How much more [verb]? · embedded: [clause] how much more [uncountable] [subject] [verb]
entries.contrast: pairs with how many more as much pairs with many. Do not confuse the determiner with the degree adverb: how much more expensive is it? modifies an adjective and is an adverb; how much more money do you need? has a noun after it and is a determiner. The rhetorical use — how much more evidence do you want? — expects no answer and means 'that is already enough.'
entries.see also: how many more, how much, how many fewer, how much less, more

entries.meaning: Asks the hearer to identify or specify the noun, with no assumption that the answer comes from a limited list.
examples: What time does the meeting start?
What books did you take with you?
What music do you listen to when you work?
What size shoe does she wear?
I never found out what excuse he gave.
What color should we paint the hallway?
What evidence do they actually have?
entries.pronunciation note: weak form /wət/ when unstressed; the final /t/ flaps into a following vowel, so what a is [ˈwʌɾə] and what is it runs to [ˈwʌɾɪzɪt]. Most Americans have the wine–whine merger and begin the word with plain /w/; older and Southern speakers keep /hwʌt/
entries.русский: какой, что за — вопрос без опоры на закрытый список (в отличие от which)
entries.position: central
entries.goes with: any noun type — singular countable (what time, what color), plural countable (what books, what options), uncountable (what music, what evidence). What it cannot do is share the slot with another central determiner: ✗ the what book, ✗ what the book, ✗ what my size. With no noun after it, it is a pronoun, not a determiner: What happened?
entries.with of: What of + noun phrase exists, but it is a fixed formal idiom meaning 'and what about' — see what of — not the determiner's partitive. The everyday partitive question uses which of: ✓ Which of these is yours?, ✗ What of these is yours?
entries.pattern: What [noun] [auxiliary] [subject] [verb]? · What [noun] [verb]? (subject question — What train leaves at six?) · [clause] what [noun] [subject] [verb] (embedded, statement order) · What [noun]! (exclamative — a separate entry)
entries.contrast: what against which is the central choice of this file. Which asks you to pick from a closed set — one both speakers can see, count, or already have in mind. What leaves the set open. On a plane: What airline do you usually fly? (any of hundreds) against Which seat is mine? (a fixed, printed list). Where the choice is spelled out as alternatives, only which is natural: ✓ Which do you want, tea or coffee? Where the field is wide open, what is natural: What music do you like? rather than which music. In a great many everyday cases both are grammatical and the difference is only how bounded the speaker takes the options to be. Remember too that embedded questions keep statement order: ✓ I asked what time it was, ✗ I asked what time was it.
entries.see also: which (interrogative), what (exclamative), what (relative), whose

entries.meaning: Asks for a complete list rather than a single item. Regional — Southern and Midland American English.
examples: What all classes are you taking this semester?
What all paperwork does the closing require?
What all questions did they ask you in the interview?
She wanted to know what all documents we needed.
What all did you buy at the hardware store?
What all has he told you about the job?
entries.pronunciation note: /ˌwʌt ˈɑl/ for the majority of Americans who merge cot and caught; the two words run together over a flap, [wʌˈɾɔl]
entries.русский: что именно, какие всё — просьба о полном перечне; диал. (юг и Мидленд США), разг.
entries.position: central — the two words fill one slot
entries.register: regional and spoken — Southern and Midland American English. Rule-governed and completely natural in those varieties, but regionally marked elsewhere and out of place in edited writing
entries.goes with: plural countable nouns and uncountable nouns in the determiner use — what all classes, what all paperwork. Not used with a singular countable. It is far more often a pronoun standing alone (What all did she say?), and that is the use most non-Southern readers will meet first.
entries.with of: Not used. ✗ what all of the classes — the ordinary partitive is which of the classes.
entries.pattern: What all [plural/uncountable noun] [auxiliary] [subject] [verb]? · What all [auxiliary] [subject] [verb]? (pronoun) · parallel regional forms: who all, which all, where all, whose all
entries.variants: who all, which all, whose all, what-all (hyphenated in dialect writing)
entries.contrast: the all adds an exhaustive-list reading that plain what does not carry: What did you buy? invites one answer, What all did you buy? asks for the whole list. This is a genuine grammatical feature of Southern and Midland English, not an error of logic — but it is dialect, so flag it as such and use what things, what sorts of things, or everything that in standard writing.
entries.see also: what (interrogative), all, y'all's

entries.term: what kind of, what sort of, what type of
entries.meaning: Asks for the category, class, or variety rather than for the individual item.
examples: What kind of car does she drive?
What kind of music do you put on when you cook?
What sort of person leaves a note like that?
What kinds of documents do I need to bring?
What type of insulation did the contractor use?
What kind of dog is that?
What kind of a question is that?
entries.pronunciation note: kind of reduces heavily to [ˈkaɪnə], and what flaps into it, so the whole phrase is commonly [wəˈkaɪnə] — what kinda car
entries.русский: какого рода, какой (по типу) — вопрос о разновидности, а не об отдельном предмете
entries.position: central — the whole phrase fills one slot, and the head noun that follows normally takes no article of its own
entries.register: neutral; what sort of leans British, what type of leans technical
entries.goes with: a following noun that is normally bare — singular countable (what kind of car), plural countable (what kind of shoes, what kinds of shoes), uncountable (what kind of music). Number agreement runs on kind, not on the head noun: what kind of dog for one category, what kinds of dogs for several. Do not insert an article: the neutral form is article-less, and what kind of a car is a marked variant that adds scorn (What kind of a question is that?).
entries.with of: Of is part of the item and is obligatory: ✗ what kind car.
entries.pattern: What kind of [bare noun] [auxiliary] [subject] [verb]? · What kinds of [plural noun] …? · What kind of [noun] is it? · What kind of a [noun] …? (scornful) · What kind [verb]? (pronoun, noun elided)
entries.variants: what sort of, what type of, what brand of, what make of, what manner of (archaic, literary)
entries.contrast: the demonstrative partners are this kind of and these kinds of — the same construction, pointing instead of asking. Against plain what: what car do you drive asks for the identity of one vehicle, what kind of car do you drive asks for the category. Against which kind of: which narrows to a set already on the table (Which kind of icing, buttercream or fondant?).
entries.see also: this kind of, these kinds of, what manner of, what (interrogative), which (interrogative)

entries.meaning: Asks for the kind, class, or nature of a thing in an elevated and archaic register — 'what kind of.'
examples: What manner of man is this, that even the winds obey him?
What manner of creature could have left tracks like these?
He wondered what manner of welcome was waiting for him at the gate.
What manner of mischief have the two of you gotten into now?
The court asked what manner of proof the state intended to offer.
What manner of people do they take us for?
entries.pronunciation note: of is the weak /əv/ and reduces further to /ə/, and the t of what flaps straight into manner, so the phrase runs to [wʌɾ ˈmænɚ ə]
entries.русский: что за, какого рода — устар., книжн. эквивалент what kind of
entries.position: central — the whole phrase fills one slot, and the noun that follows takes no article of its own
entries.register: archaic and literary. It is alive today only in deliberate period style, in the one fixed phrase what manner of man, and in mock-solemn or comic use
entries.goes with: a bare noun with no determiner of its own — singular countable (what manner of man), plural countable (what manner of creatures), uncountable (what manner of mischief). The noun is usually singular, because the fossilized phrase pulls it that way. Manner itself never pluralizes in this frame: ✗ what manners of man. And the noun cannot keep an article: ✗ what manner of a man in the neutral sense.
entries.with of: Of is part of the item and is obligatory: ✗ what manner man. Nothing partitive can be built on top of it: ✗ what manner of these.
entries.pattern: What manner of [bare noun] [auxiliary] [subject] [verb]? · What manner of [noun] [verb]? (subject question) · What manner of [noun] is this? (the fixed frame) · [clause] what manner of [noun] [subject] [verb] (embedded, statement order)
entries.variants: what kind of, what sort of, what type of (the living forms), all manner of (the statement partner), no manner of (archaic negative)
entries.where an american meets it: the King James Bible, in the verse that keeps the whole phrase in circulation — What manner of man is this, that even the winds and the sea obey him? — plus Shakespeare, hymn texts, and fantasy novels reaching for an old-sounding voice. Its declarative partner all manner of fared better and is still ordinary formal English, but the question form did not survive. In modern American prose what manner of reads as either scriptural or sarcastic: what manner of idiot is a joke, not a register choice.
entries.contrast: grammatically identical to what kind of, what sort of, what type of — same slot, same bare noun, same obligatory of. Only the register differs, and it differs enormously.
entries.see also: what kind of, what sort of, what type of, all manner of, what (interrogative), this kind of

entries.meaning: Raises a previously unaddressed item as the next topic — 'and what about …?'
examples: What of the families who were never notified?
And what of the money the committee promised?
What of the second recording — has anyone listened to it?
The plan covers the city, but what of the outlying towns?
What of those who cannot afford the fee?
What of it? Nobody was hurt.
entries.pronunciation note: of reduces to /əv/ or /ə/, and the flapped t joins it: [ˈwʌɾəv]
entries.русский: а как же…?, что же с…? — книжн., риторически вводит новую, ещё не затронутую тему
entries.position: heads its own noun phrase; the noun inside the of-phrase keeps its own determiner
entries.type: interrogative — a pronoun plus preposition, not a determiner
entries.goes with: a following of-phrase containing an already-determined noun phrase — what of the others, what of my proposal, what of it. Never a bare noun: ✗ what of children.
entries.with of: Of is the construction itself and is obligatory.
entries.pattern: What of [determined noun phrase]? · What of [it/them/that]? · And what of …? (paragraph-turning rhetorical question)
entries.contrast: listed here because it is the of-partner of interrogative what, but the important point is that it is not a partitive. Which of these is yours? genuinely selects a member from a set; What of the others? selects nothing — it means 'and what about the others,' raising them as the next topic. The everyday partitive is which of, and ✗ What of these is yours? is simply wrong. Keep it apart from the fixed dismissal What of it?, which means 'so what?'
entries.see also: which of, how many of, how much of, what (interrogative)

entries.meaning: Asks about members of the set apart from the one or ones already named.
examples: What other options do we have at this point?
Which other candidates made the short list?
What other evidence did the detective find?
What other choice did I have?
Which other branch is open on Sundays?
What other languages does she speak?
entries.pronunciation note: the flapped t of what links straight into other: [ˌwʌɾ ˈʌðɚ]
entries.русский: какие ещё, какие другие — о членах множества помимо уже названных
entries.position: what / which is the central determiner; other is a postdeterminer sitting between it and the noun
entries.goes with: plural countable nouns (what other options), uncountable nouns (what other evidence), and singular countable nouns when the sense is 'besides this one' (what other choice do I have?). Word order inside the phrase is fixed: ✗ other what options.
entries.with of: Bare what other + noun takes no of. The partitive is built on the pronoun instead — which of the others, or the plural noun which others.
entries.pattern: What other [noun] [auxiliary] [subject] [verb]? · Which other [noun] …? · What other [noun] is there? · rhetorical: What other [noun] could [subject] have [past participle]?
entries.contrast: the same open/closed split as everywhere in this file: which other implies a fixed remaining set (Which other doors did you try? — the building has a countable number of them), what other leaves the field open (What other jobs have you applied for?). The same slot is filled by a quantifier in any other and no other. In American English what other very often introduces a rhetorical question meaning 'none at all': What other choice did I have?
entries.see also: other, any other, no other, what (interrogative)

entries.meaning: Asks the hearer to pick the intended item out of a set that is already known, visible, or listed.
examples: Which gate does the flight leave from?
Which shoes should I pack, the black ones or the brown?
Which apartment is yours?
I can't remember which file I saved it in.
Which day works better for you, Tuesday or Thursday?
Which paint did you end up using on the trim?
Which of these keys opens the shed?
entries.pronunciation note: a homophone of witch for most Americans; older speakers and many Southern speakers keep the /hw-/ onset, /hwɪtʃ/. The word does not reduce — there is no weak form
entries.русский: который, какой из — выбор из известного, ограниченного набора
entries.position: central
entries.goes with: any noun type — singular countable (which gate), plural countable (which shoes), uncountable (which paint, which water). It cannot combine with another central determiner: ✗ which the gate, ✗ the which gate, ✗ which my keys. With no noun after it, it is a pronoun: Which is yours?
entries.with of: Required before another determiner or a pronoun — which of the gates, which of them. Not used before a bare noun: ✓ which gates, ✗ which of gates. In the of-construction which is a pronoun, not a determiner.
entries.pattern: Which [noun] [auxiliary] [subject] [verb]? · Which [noun] [verb]? (subject question) · Which of [the/these/my + noun]? · [clause] which [noun] [subject] [verb] (embedded, statement order) · Which [noun], [option] or [option]?
entries.contrast: which against what. Which presupposes a closed set — one the speaker and hearer can enumerate, see, or point at. What leaves the set open. Which flight are you on? assumes a printed list; What flight are you on? does not. The cleanest test is a spelled-out alternative, where only which is natural: ✓ Which do you want, tea or coffee?, and Which hand is it in? rather than ✗ what hand. Against whose, the difference is identity versus ownership: Which coat is it? against whose coat is it?
entries.see also: what (interrogative), which of, which (relative), whichever

entries.meaning: Asks the hearer to select from a set that has just been identified.
examples: Which of these keys opens the shed?
Which of the applicants did you actually interview?
Which of them do you trust?
Which of the two offers is better?
I couldn't tell you which of her books I like best.
Which of you left the door unlocked?
entries.pronunciation note: of reduces to /əv/ and, in fast speech, to /ə/ — which of them [ˈwɪtʃ ə ðəm]
entries.русский: который из, кто из — партитив; местоимение, а не определитель
entries.position: heads its own noun phrase; the noun inside the of-phrase keeps its own determiner
entries.type: interrogative (partitive — a pronoun construction, not a determiner)
entries.goes with: a definite, already-determined plural or a pronoun — which of the applicants, which of these, which of them, which of us. A two-member set takes the same frame — which of the two offers, which of the two of you. Never a bare plural: ✗ which of applicants, and never an uncountable mass: ✗ which of the money → how much of the money.
entries.with of: Of is the construction itself and is obligatory. Drop it and you are back to the determiner: which applicants.
entries.pattern: Which of [the/these/my + plural noun] [auxiliary] [subject] [verb]? · Which of [them/us/you]? · Which of the two …? · embedded: [clause] which of [noun phrase] [subject] [verb]
entries.contrast: the of test in its purest form. Which applicants did you interview? is a determiner — the noun follows directly. Which of the applicants did you interview? is a pronoun — an of-phrase follows and the noun inside keeps its own determiner. Both are correct; they differ only in whether the set has already been made definite. Against what of: which of genuinely selects, what of only raises a topic. Verb agreement follows the noun inside the of-phrase: Which of the files were deleted?
entries.see also: which (interrogative), what of, how many of, how much of, whichever

entries.meaning: Marks a high degree of the quality named by the following adjective or adverb.
examples: How long the day was!
How quickly she picked it up!
How strange that nobody mentioned it.
How cold it got last night!
How kind of you to remember.
How beautifully the room turned out.
entries.pronunciation note: carries the nuclear accent of the exclamation, and the following adjective is drawn out — How LOOONG the day was!
entries.русский: как! — восклицание о степени; ставится перед прилагательным или наречием, артикль не трогает
entries.position: fronts the clause and takes an adjective or adverb; it never enters the determiner slot at all
entries.register: neutral; the full-clause form (How long the day was!) reads as literary, and everyday speech clips it to How long! or switches to what
entries.type: degree adverb — not a determiner. It is entered here because the article rule that separates it from what is the commonest exclamative error in English
entries.goes with: an adjective or an adverb, never a noun. ✗ How a day!, ✗ How day! Because it never touches a noun, it never displaces the noun's own determiner — which is exactly why the article stays behind: How long the day was!
entries.with of: No partitive — how is not a determiner, so there is no set for it to take a part of. The of in How kind of you to remember belongs to the adjective (kind of you), not to how.
entries.pattern: How [adjective]! · How [adjective] [subject] [verb]! — How long the day was! · How [adverb] [subject] [verb]! · How [subject] [verb]! — How she suffered! · How [adjective] of [person] to [verb]! — How kind of you to remember
entries.contrast: the article rule. What is a predeterminer, so it swallows the article and brings the noun along: ✓ What a long day! How is an adverb, so it takes only the adjective, and the noun phrase keeps its own article behind it: ✓ How long the day was! Cross the two and you get the classic errors How a long day! and ✗ What long the day was! The quick test: ✗ if there is a noun in the exclamation, use what; if there is only an adjective, use how.
entries.see also: what (exclamative), what a, what an, such a, such an, how big a, how good a, how much of a

examples: I've never seen such enthusiasm from a jury.
Such problems are common in older houses.
There is no such rule in the handbook.
She spoke with such confidence that nobody questioned her.
It was done in such haste that half the forms came back blank.
Such people rarely apologize.
He gave me such good advice.

senses.head: Exclamative and intensifying
body: — marks a high degree of whatever the noun names. 2. Identifying and anaphoric — 'of that kind,' pointing back to something already described (no such rule exists). 3. Result — paired with that, it introduces the consequence of the degree.
examples: I've never seen such enthusiasm from a jury.
Such problems are common in older houses.
There is no such rule in the handbook.
She spoke with such confidence that nobody questioned her.
It was done in such haste that half the forms came back blank.
Such people rarely apologize.
He gave me such good advice.

entries.pronunciation note: weak form /sətʃ/ when unstressed, which is most of the time — such a mess runs to [sətʃəˈmɛs]
entries.русский: такой — усиление степени; «такого рода» (отсылка к названному); such … that — следствие
entries.position: predeterminer before a/an (such a mess); central determiner when it attaches straight to a bare plural or uncountable (such nonsense)
entries.goes with: plural countable nouns (such problems) and uncountable nouns (such nonsense, such enthusiasm) directly. A singular countable noun requires a/an: ✓ such a mess, ✗ such mess — see such a, such an. It can never follow an article: ✗ a such mess, ✗ the such problems.
entries.with of: Not used in ordinary English. The partitive such of the + noun + as … survives only in legal drafting (such of the funds as remain unspent).
entries.pattern: such [plural noun] · such [uncountable] · such a/an [singular noun] · such [noun] that [clause] (result) · such [noun] as [noun/clause] (identifying, and the formal fused relative such money as I had) · no such [noun] (anaphoric)
entries.variants: such a, such an, no such, such as, suchlike (dialectal and dated)
entries.contrast: such against what. Both are predeterminers taking the same slot and obeying the same article rule, but what is confined to exclamations and questions while such also runs in ordinary statements: ✓ I've never seen such enthusiasm, ✗ I've never seen what enthusiasm. Such against so: so takes an adjective with no noun (so cold), such takes a noun (such cold weather) — hence ✗ so cold weather and ✗ such cold. The formal fused relative such money as I had is the older twin of what (relative).
entries.see also: such a, such an, such other, what (exclamative), what (relative), no such

entries.meaning: Marks a single countable thing or person as extreme, remarkable, or exactly of that kind.
examples: It was such a long day.
He's such an idiot about money.
Such a shame the weather turned.
She's such a good listener.
It was such a mess that we gave up and ordered takeout.
I've never met such an honest salesman.
entries.pronunciation note: both words normally reduce: such a [sətʃə], such an [sətʃən]
entries.русский: такой — усиление перед исчисляемым ед. ч.; such стоит перед a/an: such a mess
entries.position: predeterminer — such stands in front of the indefinite article, which then does its ordinary job on the noun
entries.goes with: singular countable nouns only — such a day, such an idiot. Never a plural (✗ such a problems → such problems), never an uncountable (✗ such a nonsense → such nonsense), and never with the definite article (✗ such the day).
entries.with of: None.
entries.pattern: such a/an [(adjective) singular countable noun] · such a/an [noun] that [clause] · such a/an [noun] as [noun/clause] · exclamative: Such a [noun]!
entries.contrast: the article-order rule in its most-tested form: ✓ such a long day, ✗ a such long day. It matches what a long day exactly, and contrasts with how long the day was, where no noun is involved and the article therefore stays behind. Against so: ✓ so long a day (formal) and ✓ such a long day, but ✗ so a long day and ✗ such long a day. Choose an by sound, not spelling: such an hour, such a union.
entries.see also: such, what a, what an, how (exclamative), an

entries.meaning: 'The remaining ones of that kind, whichever they turn out to be' — a drafting formula that leaves a category open and then closes it with an as-clause.
examples: The tenant shall pay rent, utilities, and such other charges as the lease may specify.
Plaintiff prays for damages, costs, and such other and further relief as the Court deems just.
The board may appoint a treasurer and such other officers as it considers necessary.
I leave my house, my car, and such other property as I may own at my death to my sister.
The contractor shall furnish the permits and such other documents as the architect reasonably requests.
Employees receive health coverage and such other benefits as the company provides from time to time.
entries.pronunciation note: such takes its weak form /sətʃ/ here, because the accent runs forward to the noun — such other TERMS, such other RELIEF
entries.русский: прочие такие, иные подобные — юр., договорная формула, обычно с оборотом as …
entries.position: such fills the central slot and other is a postdeterminer between it and the noun
entries.register: legal and contractual. This is drafting boilerplate, not ordinary English; used outside a document it sounds like an impression of a lawyer
entries.goes with: plural countable nouns (such other terms, such other documents) and uncountable nouns (such other relief, such other property). A singular countable would need a/an and the frame does not take it — drafters write any other case, not ✗ such other a case. It can never follow an article: ✗ the such other terms, ✗ a such other document.
entries.with of: Not used. The drafting partitive is a different frame, such of the + noun + as — such of the funds as remain unspent — and there such is a pronoun, not a determiner.
entries.pattern: such other [plural/uncountable noun] as [clause] — the as-tail is all but obligatory · such other and further [noun] as … (the fixed doublet) · such other [noun] as the [party] may [verb] · and for such other relief as the Court deems just and proper (the fixed closing of an American pleading)
entries.variants: such other and further, any other (the plain-English replacement), such … as
entries.where an american actually meets it: three places, all of them documents — a contract's catch-all clause, the prayer for relief at the end of a complaint, and a will.
entries.contrast: against what other, which other, which ask about the remaining members of a set; such other asserts them and then defines them with an as-clause. Against bare such, which points back to a kind already described: such other points to the rest of that kind — everything answering the description that has not already been listed. Its whole value to a drafter is that the as-clause can leave the category open-ended without naming a single member, which is also why plain-language style guides tell drafters to write any other instead.
entries.see also: such, what other, which other, other, no such

entries.meaning: Registers a strong reaction to the noun — admiration, dismay, scorn, or surprise.
examples: What beautiful flowers!
What nonsense — none of that is in the contract.
What nerve that man has!
What luck, running into you here.
What terrible timing.
What lovely manners those children have.
entries.pronunciation note: carries the accent of the exclamation; the /t/ flaps into a following vowel, so what an idiot is [wʌɾənˈaɪɾiət]
entries.русский: какой!, что за! — восклицание-реакция: восторг, ужас, презрение или удивление
entries.position: predeterminer in front of a/an (what a mess!); central determiner when it attaches straight to a bare plural or uncountable (what nonsense!) — the same two-slot behavior as such
entries.goes with: plural countable nouns (What beautiful flowers!) and uncountable nouns (What nonsense!, What luck!) directly. A singular countable requires a/an and is treated at what a, what an: ✗ What mess! → ✓ What a mess! It never combines with the: ✗ What the flowers!
entries.with of: Not used in exclamations. The formal idiom what of is a question, not an exclamation.
entries.pattern: What [plural noun]! · What [uncountable]! · What [(adjective) noun] [subject] [verb]! — What nerve that man has! · What [noun] to [verb]! · embedded: [clause] what [noun] [subject] [verb]
entries.contrast: against how (exclamative), apply the noun test: a noun in the exclamation means what, an adjective alone means how. Against such, which fills the same slot in ordinary statements rather than exclamations. Against interrogative what, which is identical in form and separated only by intonation and by word order — the question inverts (What time is it?), the exclamation does not (What time we had!).
entries.see also: what a, what an, how (exclamative), such, what (interrogative)

entries.meaning: Registers a strong reaction to a single countable thing or person.
examples: What a long day!
What an idiot I've been.
What a mess the kitchen is.
What a week we've had.
What an honor to be asked.
What a way to find out.
entries.pronunciation note: almost always flapped in running speech: [ˈwʌɾə], [ˈwʌɾən] — what a mess is [wʌɾəˈmɛs]
entries.русский: какой!, что за! — восклицание об исчисляемом ед. ч.; what стоит перед a/an
entries.position: predeterminer — what stands in front of a/an
entries.goes with: singular countable nouns only — what a day, what an honor. ✗ what a flowers, ✗ what a nonsense. With plurals and uncountables the article simply disappears: see what (exclamative). It never takes the definite article: ✗ what the day.
entries.with of: None.
entries.pattern: What a/an [(adjective) singular noun]! · What a/an [noun] [subject] [verb]! — What a day I've had! · What a/an [noun] to [verb]! · embedded: [clause] what a [noun] [subject] [verb]
entries.contrast: the article-placement rule at its clearest: ✓ What a long day!, ✗ What long a day!, ✗ A what long day! Against how, which never touches a noun and so leaves the article behind: ✓ How long the day was! Choose an by sound: what an hour to call, what a European mess. Note the sarcasm American English gets out of it — said flatly, What a friend is an insult, and What a question! usually means the question was foolish.
entries.see also: what (exclamative), such a, such an, how (exclamative), a

entries.meaning: Concedes a small amount or number without settling on one — 'no matter how little.'
examples: However little money you start with, the closing costs add up.
However few options are left, we still have to choose one.
He'll find something to complain about, however little work you give him.
However few people show up, the reading goes ahead.
She made do with however little counter space the kitchen had.
However few hours he sleeps, he's up at five.
However little of the budget survives, the audit still has to happen.
entries.pronunciation note: written as one word in this use; the t of little is a flap in General American, so it comes out how-EV-er-LID-ul
entries.русский: как бы мало ни — уступка о малом количестве (little — неисчисл., few — счётные)
entries.position: central — the two words fill one slot
entries.register: neutral to formal; less frequent than however much and however many
entries.goes with: however little + uncountable (however little money, however little time); however few + plural countable (however few options, however few people). The split is the ordinary little/few split, so ✗ however little options and ✗ however few money, and neither takes a singular countable (✗ however few option). With no noun following, however little is a degree adverb (however little it matters), not a determiner.
entries.with of: Partitive however little of the / however few of the is possible, and of is required before a pronoun (however few of them, however little of it). The wh- word is a pronoun in that construction. Never before a bare plural: ✗ however few of options.
entries.pattern: However little [uncountable] [subject] [verb], [main clause] · However few [plural noun] [subject] [verb], [main clause] · [main clause], however little [uncountable] [subject] [verb] · however few of [them/the + plural noun] · however little [subject] [verb] (adverb, no noun)
entries.variants: no matter how little, no matter how few
entries.contrast: the negatively loaded twin of however much, however many. However much money you have concedes an amount of any size; however little money you have concedes that the amount is small and says it makes no difference. The quantifier is bare little and bare few, never the a-forms: ✗ however a little money, ✗ however a few options. Against interrogative how little and how few, which ask about the quantity instead of conceding it, and against the fused relatives what little and what few, which assert a small quantity rather than waiving it.
entries.see also: however much, however many, how little, how few, what little, what few

entries.meaning: Concedes any amount or number without settling on one — 'no matter what amount of.'
examples: However much money you throw at it, the roof will still leak.
However many times I explain it, he asks again.
Take however many copies you need.
However much patience I start with, that meeting drains it.
They'll seat you, however many people you bring.
Spend however much time you want on the draft.
entries.pronunciation note: written as one word in this use; the two-word how ever is a different, emphatic interrogative and is stressed how EV-er
entries.русский: сколько бы ни — уступка о любом количестве (much — неисчисл., many — счётные)
entries.position: central — the whole phrase fills one slot
entries.goes with: however much + uncountable (however much money); however many + plural countable (however many times). The countability split is the ordinary much/many split, so ✗ however much times and ✗ however many money. With no noun following, however much is a degree adverb (however much it costs), not a determiner.
entries.with of: Partitive however much of the / however many of the is possible, and of is required before a pronoun (however many of them). The wh- word is a pronoun in that construction.
entries.pattern: However much [uncountable] [subject] [verb], [main clause] · However many [plural noun] [subject] [verb], [main clause] · [main clause] however much [uncountable] [subject] [verb] · [verb] however many [plural noun] [subject] [verb] · however much [subject] [verb] (adverb, no noun)
entries.variants: no matter how much, no matter how many, how ever much (emphatic, two words)
entries.contrast: concessive, not interrogative: it does not ask, it concedes. However much money you throw at it means 'no matter what amount of money.' Keep it apart from however the connective adverb, which is followed by a comma and no noun (However, the flight was canceled), and from the emphatic two-word how ever (How ever did you manage?). Against whatever, which concedes without measuring: whatever excuses he gives names the kind, however many excuses he gives counts them. The negatively loaded twins are however little and however few.
entries.see also: however little, however few, whatever, whichever, how much, how many

entries.meaning: Hooks a following clause onto the situation just described, naming that situation with a noun.
examples: The flight may be canceled, in which case we'll drive.
He arrived at noon, by which time we had already left.
The tenant may refuse, at which point the matter goes to arbitration.
She could still appeal, in which event the hearing would be reopened.
The check might bounce, in which case you'll hear from me.
We waited until Friday, by which time the offer had expired.
entries.pronunciation note: the noun takes the accent — at which POINT, by which TIME
entries.русский: в таком случае — цепляет следующую фразу к только что описанной ситуации
entries.position: which is the central determiner of the noun, inside a fronted prepositional phrase; the phrase as a whole opens its clause
entries.register: neutral to formal; standard in careful writing, contracts, and business speech
entries.goes with: a small closed set of abstract nouns naming a situation, moment, or reason — case, point, time, event, instance, circumstances, reason, occasion, juncture, stage, respect. It cannot take an ordinary concrete noun in this relative use: ✗ He sat down, in which chair we later found his keys, ✗ by which sandwich. (The interrogative In which chair did he sit? is a different construction and is fine.)
entries.with of: None — the preposition is already supplied by the phrase itself (in, at, by, for, after, during, since).
entries.pattern: [clause], in which case [clause] · [clause], at which point [clause] · [clause], by which time [clause] · [clause], for which reason [clause] · the same phrases also open a new sentence as a connector
entries.variants: at which point, by which time, at which time, in which event, for which reason, on which occasion, during which time, since which date, after which
entries.contrast: the antecedent here is not a noun but the whole preceding clause — He arrived at noon, by which time we had left: which time reaches back and names the moment the first clause established. This is the one place where relative which works comfortably as a determiner in everyday American English; elsewhere the determiner use (He offered a settlement, which offer we declined) is legal or archaic. It cannot introduce a restrictive clause: ✗ the meeting in which case we voted. And it takes a comma in front of it — running it on without one is the standard error.
entries.see also: which (relative), which (interrogative), of which

entries.meaning: Archaic which, with the definite article still standing in front of it — alone as a relative pronoun, or, less often, before a noun as a relative determiner.
examples: He came at midnight, at the which hour the gates were already shut. (determiner)
They sailed to a far country, in the which land no man knew them. (determiner)
She made him a promise, the which she never kept. (pronoun — the ordinary older use)
The king granted him a charter, by the which grant the town was made free. (determiner)
He fell into a great sickness, from the which he never recovered. (pronoun)
There was a famine in the land, for the which cause they went down into Egypt. (determiner)
entries.pronunciation note: the is the ordinary weak /ðə/ in front of the consonant /w/, never /ði/; /hwɪtʃ/ for speakers who keep the wh- onset. In verse the article can be elided to th' for the meter, th' which
entries.русский: который, каковой — устар. (совр. which с определённым артиклем впереди)
entries.position: the and which together fill the central slot when a noun follows (the which time); with no noun after it the pair is a pronoun and holds no determiner slot at all
entries.register: obsolete in every variety of modern English — Middle and Early Modern English only
entries.type: relative — archaic. A relative pronoun in most of its attested uses and a relative determiner in the minority of them; it is entered here for that minority
entries.goes with: in the determiner use, chiefly the same small set of abstract nouns that modern relative which still takes — the which time, the which place, the which cause, the which thing — and, in Middle English, a wider range of ordinary nouns besides. In modern English no noun is possible at all: ✗ the which gate, ✗ the which report. Far more often nothing follows and the phrase is simply a relative pronoun meaning which.
entries.with of: The construction is already built on an article, so of attaches outside it, in the older genitive frame of the which — the direct ancestor of today's of which. There is no partitive: ✗ the which of these.
entries.pattern: [clause], the which [verb] … (pronoun — the commonest use by far) · [clause], [preposition] the which [noun] [clause] — in the which place, at the which time (determiner) · [clause], the which [noun] [verb] (determiner, subject) · the modern equivalents are plain which, or in which case and its siblings
entries.variants: which (the living form), the whiche (Middle English spelling), of the which (the older of which)
entries.where an american meets it: Chaucer and other Middle English texts, Spenser, Shakespeare, and a scattering of places in the King James Bible, where it alternates freely with plain which for no reason a modern reader can detect. It is a period marker rather than a style option — recognize it, never write it.
entries.contrast: this is the construction behind the ✗ mark in which (interrogative): the which gate is impossible today, but the which was ordinary English for three centuries. Modern which carries its own definiteness; Middle English still spelled that definiteness out with an article in front, exactly as French does with lequel. The determiner reading survives in fossil form in in which case and at which point, which are the same idea with the article dropped.
entries.see also: which (relative), in which case, which (interrogative), of which

entries.meaning: 'The (little) X that' — packages a noun together with its relative clause into a single phrase, with the quantity implied to be limited.
examples: He spent what money he had on the repair.
She sold what furniture would fit in the truck.
What evidence remains is inconclusive.
Take what supplies you need from the closet.
They saved what photographs survived the flood.
I'll give you what help I can.
entries.pronunciation note: weak form /wət/, since the fused relative is rarely accented — what money I had runs to [wətˈmʌni]
entries.русский: то (немногое), что — сращённое относительное: what money I had «те деньги, что у меня были»
entries.position: central
entries.register: neutral, with a slightly literary edge
entries.type: relative (fused relative — it contains its own antecedent)
entries.goes with: uncountable nouns (what money I had) and plural countable nouns (what photographs survived). A bare singular countable is marginal and normally rephrased (✗? what car I owned → the car I owned). The noun is nearly always small in quantity — the construction carries an undertone of 'the little there was,' which is why the fixed expansions what little and what few exist.
entries.with of: None in the determiner use. what of is a separate, non-determiner idiom and means something else entirely.
entries.pattern: what [noun] [subject] [verb] — what money I had · [verb] what [noun] [subject] [verb] — He spent what savings he had · what [noun] [verb] — What evidence remains is inconclusive · expansions: what little [uncountable], what few [plural]
entries.variants: what little, what few, such … as (the formal older equivalent)
entries.nonstandard warning: the relative pronoun what in the book what I read is a well-established feature of several British and American vernaculars and is entirely systematic there, but it is not standard written English — use that or which.
entries.contrast: the fused relative has no antecedent — it supplies its own. What money I had is a complete noun phrase meaning 'the money that I had.' Relative which and relative whose both require an antecedent already standing in the sentence (the money which I had). Against interrogative what, the test is whether an answer is being requested: I asked what money he had embeds a question, He spent what money he had asks nothing.
entries.see also: what little, what few, whatever, such

entries.meaning: 'The few X that' — names a small remaining number and attaches its clause in one phrase.
examples: What few friends he had left stopped calling.
She used what few vacation days she had on the funeral.
What few records survived are in the county archive.
They spent what few dollars remained on gas.
What few options we have are all expensive.
He answered what few questions he could.
entries.pronunciation note: the accent falls on few
entries.русский: те немногие, что — о малом оставшемся числе счётных: what few friends he had
entries.position: central — the two words fill one slot
entries.goes with: plural countable nouns only — what few friends I have, what few options remain. Never an uncountable (✗ what few money → what little money) and never a singular countable.
entries.with of: None. ✗ what few of the friends I have — the partitive would be the few of my friends who …
entries.pattern: what few [plural noun] [subject] [verb] · what few [plural noun] [verb] · [verb] what few [plural noun] [subject] [verb]
entries.contrast: the plural-countable partner of what little, and a fixed expansion of fused-relative what. The few keeps its usual negative loading — 'not many, and that is the point' — so what few friends I have asserts that the number is small. The a-form is impossible here: ✗ what a few friends. Do not confuse it with interrogative how few, which asks about the number instead of asserting it.
entries.see also: what little, what (relative), few, how few

entries.meaning: 'The little X that' — names a small remaining amount and attaches its clause in one phrase.
examples: He gave what little money he had to the driver.
What little time remains should go to the conclusion.
She salvaged what little dignity she could.
What little evidence there is points the other way.
They shared what little food was left in the pack.
I'll offer what little advice I have.
entries.pronunciation note: the t of little is a flap, so it comes out wuht-LID-ul
entries.русский: то немногое, что — о малом оставшемся объёме неисчисляемого: what little time we had
entries.position: central — the two words fill one slot
entries.goes with: uncountable nouns only — what little time remains, what little money he had. Never a plural countable (✗ what little friends → what few friends).
entries.with of: None.
entries.pattern: what little [uncountable] [subject] [verb] · what little [uncountable] [verb] · [verb] what little [uncountable] [subject] [verb]
entries.contrast: the uncountable partner of what few. The quantifier is bare little, the negative-loading form, never a little: ✗ what a little money. Against interrogative how little, which asks about the amount rather than asserting it. Against plain what (relative), what little simply makes the small quantity explicit.
entries.see also: what few, what (relative), little, how little

examples: Take whatever seat you like.
Whatever excuse he gives, I'm not covering for him again.
Spend whatever money is left in the account.
She reads whatever books the library has on the subject.
Whatever problems the merger creates, they'll be somebody else's.
Bring whatever tools you think you'll need.

senses.head: Fused relative
body: — 'any X that,' supplying its own antecedent: Take whatever seat you like. 2. Concessive — 'no matter what X': Whatever excuse he gives, I don't believe it. 3. Emphatic interrogative — adds exasperation to a question (Whatever reason could she have had?); chiefly British in this determiner use, where Americans say what on earth. 4. Postposed emphasizer after a negative — no reason whatever.
examples: Take whatever seat you like.
Whatever excuse he gives, I'm not covering for him again.
Spend whatever money is left in the account.
She reads whatever books the library has on the subject.
Whatever problems the merger creates, they'll be somebody else's.
Bring whatever tools you think you'll need.

entries.pronunciation note: the /t/ flaps, so the ordinary American pronunciation is [wəˈɾɛvɚ]; the dismissive interjection whatever is stressed differently, WHAT-ever
entries.русский: любой какой угодно; какой бы ни — сращённое относительное и уступительное «неважно какой»
entries.position: central
entries.type: relative (fused relative) and concessive; also emphatic interrogative
entries.goes with: any noun type — singular countable (whatever excuse he gives), plural countable (whatever books you want), uncountable (whatever money is left). It cannot share the slot with another central determiner: ✗ the whatever excuse.
entries.with of: Not used in the determiner sense. Whatever of + noun phrase exists but is archaic; the living partitive is whichever of the …
entries.pattern: whatever [noun] [subject] [verb], [main clause] (concessive) · [verb] whatever [noun] [subject] [verb] (fused relative, object) · whatever [noun] [verb] (fused relative, subject) · Whatever [noun] [auxiliary] [subject] [verb]? (emphatic question) · [noun] whatever (postposed emphasizer after a negative)
entries.variants: whatsoever (emphatic and archaic), no matter what (the everyday spoken equivalent), what ever (two words, in the emphatic question)
entries.contrast: whatever against whichever repeats the what/which split exactly: whatever leaves the set open (whatever books you want — from anywhere at all), whichever picks from a set already fixed (whichever of these two you want). Determiner against pronoun: a noun follows the determiner (whatever seat), nothing follows the pronoun (take whatever you like). Whatever also runs as a free-choice quantifier meaning 'any at all, it makes no difference' (call me whatever day suits you), which puts it next to any in meaning; the grammar is the same fused relative in every case, so the word is catalogued here.
entries.see also: whichever, whatsoever, what (relative), any

entries.meaning: Strengthens a negation to 'not the smallest amount of' — or, archaically, 'any … at all that.'
examples: There is no evidence whatsoever to support that claim.
She has no interest whatsoever in running for office.
I have no doubt whatsoever that he meant it.
Do you have any objection whatsoever?
The policy makes no exception whatsoever for late filings.
Whatsoever things are true, think on these things.
entries.pronunciation note: four syllables, accent on ev; the t does not flap here because /s/ follows
entries.русский: вообще никакой, ни малейшего — усилитель после отрицания; устар. «какой бы ни»
entries.position: postposed in the modern use — it follows the noun it strengthens and therefore never occupies the determiner slot at all. In the archaic relative use it precedes the noun
entries.register: formal and emphatic; the relative use is biblical or legal
entries.type: emphatic negative-polarity item; also, archaically, a fused relative
entries.goes with: a noun already determined by no, any, none, or little — no evidence whatsoever, any doubt whatsoever, nothing whatsoever. It is a negative-polarity item: a negative or a question has to license it, so ✗ He has some evidence whatsoever. In the archaic fused-relative use it takes a bare plural or uncountable ahead of it (whatsoever things are true).
entries.with of: None.
entries.pattern: no [noun] whatsoever · not … any [noun] whatsoever · none whatsoever · nothing/nobody whatsoever · archaic: whatsoever [noun] [subject] [verb]
entries.variants: whatever (the same postposed emphasizer, slightly less formal: no reason whatever), at all (the everyday spoken equivalent), whatsoe'er (poetic)
entries.contrast: against whatever: the postposed emphasizer is the same word in a different slot, and whatsoever is the more emphatic and more formal of the two. It is licensed by the same negatives catalogued in no and not any, and it strengthens them rather than negating anything itself. The archaic relative — whatsoever things are true — is a fused relative exactly like whatever, and today survives only in scripture, hymnody, and legal boilerplate.
entries.see also: whatever, whichsoever, not any, no

entries.meaning: Carries the antecedent — often a whole clause — forward into a following clause by naming it with a noun.
examples: He arrived at noon, by which time we had already left.
The tenant may object, at which point the matter goes to arbitration.
She refused the offer, for which reason the sale collapsed.
They proposed a settlement, which offer my client declined.
Payment may be late, in which event a fee applies.
He was in Denver until Friday, during which time the office stayed closed.
entries.pronunciation note: unreduced even though unstressed; /hwɪtʃ/ for speakers who keep the wh- onset
entries.русский: каковой, этот самый — книжн.: подхватывает сказанное (by which time, at which point)
entries.position: central, normally inside a fronted prepositional phrase
entries.register: formal; only in which case and its siblings are ordinary in everyday American English
entries.goes with: abstract nouns naming a time, point, case, event, or reason, in a supplementary (nonrestrictive) clause — by which time, at which point, in which case, for which reason. Beyond that closed set the determiner use survives only in legal and older formal prose, where it can take almost any noun that repeats or reclassifies the antecedent: He made an offer, which offer we declined.
entries.with of: of which is a different construction — a relative genitive that names something the antecedent has, not this determiner. Compare a house the roof of which leaks (genitive) with he left at noon, by which time we had gone (determiner).
entries.pattern: [clause], [preposition] which [noun] [clause] · [clause], which [noun] [verb] (legal or archaic) · nonrestrictive only, and a comma is required in front
entries.variants: in which case, at which point, by which time, for which reason
entries.contrast: determiner which against pronoun which. The pronoun stands alone and is the everyday relative (the report, which arrived late); the determiner has a noun immediately after it (he left at noon, by which time the deadline had passed). The determiner cannot introduce a restrictive clause at all: ✗ the moment which time we left. Against that: American usage reserves that for restrictive clauses and comma-which for nonrestrictive ones, and since the determiner use is nonrestrictive by nature, that is never an option. Against relative whose, which marks possession rather than repeating the antecedent as a noun.
entries.see also: in which case, the which, which (interrogative), of which, whose

entries.meaning: 'Any one of the known set that' — picks freely inside a set already established, or concedes the choice to someone else.
examples: Take whichever seat you like.
Whichever route we take, we'll hit traffic.
Use whichever card has room on it.
Whichever candidate wins, the policy won't change.
Pick whichever two days work for you.
Whichever of the two offers you accept, get it in writing.
entries.pronunciation note: three syllables, accent on ev; the two-word which ever (emphatic interrogative) is chiefly British
entries.русский: какой угодно из; какой бы ни — свободный выбор внутри уже известного набора
entries.position: central
entries.goes with: singular countable (whichever route we take), plural countable (whichever seats are free), and, less often, uncountable (whichever paint you prefer). Like every central determiner it cannot stack with another: ✗ the whichever route.
entries.with of: Required before another determiner or a pronoun — whichever of the two, whichever of them. Whichever is a pronoun in that construction, not a determiner. Never before a bare plural: ✗ whichever of routes.
entries.pattern: whichever [noun] [subject] [verb] · whichever [noun] [verb] · whichever of [the/these + plural noun] · [clause], whichever [subject] [verb] (concessive) · whichever comes first (fixed contractual tag, pronoun)
entries.variants: whichsoever (archaic and legal), no matter which (spoken), which ever (two words, emphatic interrogative)
entries.contrast: whichever against whatever repeats the which/what split exactly: whichever selects inside a set already fixed (whichever of these two rooms), whatever leaves it open (whatever room is free). Determiner against pronoun: whichever route has a noun after it, take whichever you like does not. Note the fixed legal tag whichever comes first, where whichever stands alone as a pronoun. The free-choice use — use whichever card you like — sits alongside any in meaning but keeps the fused-relative grammar described here.
entries.see also: whatever, whichsoever, which (interrogative), any

entries.meaning: Archaic emphatic form of whichever — 'any one at all of the set that.' ---
examples: Whichsoever party breaches first shall bear the costs.
The estate passes to whichsoever heir survives the longer.
Whichsoever terms the arbitrator sets are binding on both.
He vowed to follow whichsoever road led home.
Whichsoever of the two dates is chosen, notice must be given.
Whichsoever course ye take, take it wholeheartedly.
entries.pronunciation note: four syllables, accent on ev
entries.русский: какой бы ни (из) — устар., юр. усиленная форма whichever
entries.position: central
entries.register: archaic — it survives only in legal boilerplate, scripture, and deliberate period style
entries.goes with: singular and plural countable nouns inside a free relative clause — whichsoever party, whichsoever terms. Uncountables are possible but vanishingly rare.
entries.with of: Whichsoever of the + plural noun, as a pronoun; of is required before a determiner or a pronoun, exactly as with whichever.
entries.pattern: whichsoever [noun] [subject] [verb] · whichsoever of [the + plural noun] · [clause] whichsoever [noun] [verb]
entries.variants: whichever (the living form), whatsoever, whosoever, whosesoever and the two-word whose soever (the genitive members — catalogued at whosever), whensoever
entries.contrast: an intensified whichever, built the same way whatsoever is built from whatever. In modern American English it is not a stylistic option, it is a period marker — use whichever. It is entered here so a reader can recognize it in a deed, an insurance policy, or the King James Bible.
entries.see also: whichever, whatsoever, whosever
